I honestly fell asleep the first watch through, so I had to watch it again. This is my first time watching either Aladdin, so I don't feel disturbed as others might feel about all the additions, replacements, and whatever. I felt like this version did a better—but not good—job of respecting the culture in the Middle East. The women aren't as hypersexualized in this version as it was in the original animation, straying away from Orientalism just a bit. In fact, everyone is a lot more clothed than shown in the animation. However, I'm no expert, but I've noticed that rather than representing the Middle East, there were many Indian elements like the clothes in the movie. I'm glad they didn't make Jasmine look like the typical belly dancer stereotype, but they still failed to depict what Arabian women would actually wear. Moreover, Jasmine was able to jump with the pole in the original as she was running away with Aladdin, which showed some of her fearlessness (that ultimately never got fleshed out), but in this one, she chickens out. That pissed me off because if they're trying to empower Jasmine, there was no reason to make her back out in this scene. Also, there was no need to leave her frozen in place at such a critical moment, where she could've proven herself. Sadly, the men have to save this damsel in distress once more. What surprised me the most was The Sultan having more aura in this movie. In the original, this guy was just an idiot with almost no thought of his own, but in this one, he tried to stand his ground. I guess they donated some of Jasmine's fearlessness to a man who doesn't even have a name. I really don't care if they bring some random handmaiden into the movie, but if they can make changes like that, I would've loved if they removed more of the harmful stereotypes and made Jasmine independent. It honestly feels like they watered down the original to make it seem less problematic when, really, the true meaning and intent are still there. There are several Israel sympathizers in the cast as well that have also played violent roles in other media. Yes, there's a more diverse cast that come from the Middle East but at what cost? The soundtrack did have bangers, but it sounded more Western than Middle Eastern. For example, when Jasmine played that one instrument, it just sounded like a regular guitar you'd hear in the US. When you look at the composers behind these songs, you'll quickly notice that none of them are Arab; it all adds up. As I talked about earlier with things being watered down, the lyrics to "Arabian Nights" were tweaked to make the people seem less barbaric in Arabia, but they still call them barbaric. Overall, the movie definitely made some nice changes from the original, but they weren't done right. This could've been so much better.

“He’s a little dim, but you’re just getting married. It’s not like you have to talk to him.” Guy Ritchie’s remake of the 1992 animated classic follows Aladdin as he discovers a magic lamp that contains a genie who helps him impress Princess Jasmine of Agrabah by disguising him as a prince, only to raise the suspicion of the evil vizier Jafar. Another unnecessary remake thats only success lies in the portrayal of the Genie that toed a line between a fresh take and homage, with Jasmine’s handmaiden Dalia - Genie’s future wife - a decent new character who didn’t detract from the story. Their chemistry surpassed Aladdin and Jasmine’s with much less time spent together throughout. At its worst when it’s copying the original as the flaws become glaring, especially in the portrayal of Jafar who was neither menacing nor effective as a conjurer even with the full power of the lamp. The songs were uninspiring and lacked any magic from “A Whole New World” to “Friend Like Me” to Jasmine’s new song “Speechless” that succeeds in showing off her voice while still being lacking. Cast includes Mena Massoud, Naomi Scott, Will Smith, Marwan Kenzari, Navid Negahban, Nasim Pedrad, Billy Magnussen, and Alan Tudyk as Iago, with Frank Welker the lone returnee voicing Abu.

I was surprised it starts in the ocean and frames itself as a "tale" now; you can tell they're trying to distance themselves from the original. I did find it interesting how the opening says "chaotic" instead of "barbaric" and they mention culture and tradition. The world is much tamer now as there are trees, no exaggerated violence or features, and when the merchant accuses Jasmine of stealing, he just wants her bracelet instead of threatening to cut off her hand. They clearly tried to fix the stereotypes. But Jasmine did disappoint me. She's no longer as brave or confident as she was in the original and ironically male reliant. She's too scared to do the pole jump and Aladdin catches her in his lap which is very odd, especially since she impresses Aladdin all on her own in the original. She's lying about her identity and just seems more confused and a muddy character. She already knew her value in the original, but here her "empowerment" feels forced. She did get her own song though which is different, but I didn't really like it and gave defendants vibes. What is cool though is the Sultan is more of a leader and keeps Jafar in check but he's not really in the movie. Will Smith as the Genie was alright; I don't really have much of an opinion on that, but I did not like the subplot with the handmaid as it was odd and didn't really add anything to the story. The acting was just kinda bad in general. I do like how the women aren't sexualized in this movie, especially Jasmine at the end. You can really see they tried not to be racist, but it feels like a corporate checklist imo.

The movie is entertaining and the musical numbers are really enjoyable. I especially liked seeing the original story brought to life in a more modern way. It’s definitely not as magical as the original, which will always be hard to beat, but I still really enjoyed watching it. A fun and colorful remake that I’d happily watch again.

A live action that comes off more like a Broadway show that ended up in the wrong place. And that pretty much explains everything that doesn't work. There's a whole musical number shoved into the middle of the film that plays out like a Disney park parade, way more than anything that matters to the story. The CGI is overdone and bad. The problem isn't the target audience, a teen adventure in the same lane as Descendants and Zombies . It's the quality of the production as a whole, even with the effort of putting a superstar like Will Smith in the cast. There are a few isolated stretches of decent rom com, but nothing you haven't seen before. Another thing that stands out, compared to the original cartoon, is how much time Will Smith spends as a human and builds a relationship with Dalia, Jasmine's handmaiden. That's not in the original at all. And what's holding up what little quality is left is the soundtrack, excellent as always in Disney films, which only proves the point: when the music is the only standout in a movie, maybe it should've just stayed on a stage.

It was always a tall order for Will Smith to step into Robin Williams’ iconic role. But if you give him the grace of imagining casting another big personality (albeit from music as opposed to comedy) Smith is a strong choice and he DOES A GOOD JOB. The real problem is Guy Ritchie having not one iota of interest or imagination to do anything but phone in his version of this story. The “One Jump” and “Prince Ali” sequences betray an utter lack of creativity on Ritchie’s part. A shame because other aspects of this film are strong enough to have made an impact in another life.
